title: Team Size and Composition

know: Larson's sizing rules of thumb — about six to eight engineers per manager, about eight for a two-tier on-call rotation, teams below four not functioning as teams — and the reasoning behind each.
The composition of a product team: engineering, product, design and, where needed, data.
What a smaller team gains and gives up.
believe: A team size is the result of a derivation from load, on-call and coordination cost, and has to be re-derived when one of them changes.
can_do: Derive a size for a team with a given scope and on-call duty.
Say whether a team that is too small should grow, shed scope or merge.
State the assumptions under which a rule of thumb they use holds.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a team's scope, on-call duty and current size, the reader says whether the size is right and which of three remedies applies, with the reason.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A team of four owns three customer-facing services with a 24/7 on-call duty; two of the four are on call every second week. Using only this chapter: is four the right size, and what are the options?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No: four cannot sustain the rotation (Larson's rule of thumb is about eight for two tiers); the options are to grow, to shed or share scope and on-call with another team, or to merge; adding scope-free headcount elsewhere does not help.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter's closing synthesizes Part II and reads Corvane's platform team as a type, a mode and a size.
Larson's numbers are presented as his rules of thumb with their stated reasons, not as laws, and the chapter says what each assumes.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: How large should a team be and who should be in it, derived from load, on-call and coordination cost?
thesis.claim: A team should be as large as three things require and no larger: enough people to understand and change what it owns without depending on one of them, enough to sustain its on-call rotation, and few enough that it can coordinate without splitting into sub-teams — which for teams that write and operate their own services gives Larson's six to eight engineers with one manager, and which gives a different number when the scope, the on-call duty or the cost of producing a change is different; the team's composition follows the same logic, bringing product, design and engineering together wherever a decision would otherwise wait for another team.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that smaller teams are faster, so teams should be kept as small as possible (the two-pizza rule), and the opposite planning habit of sizing teams by the budget available.
thesis.so_what: A leader states the assumptions behind a team's size, grows, shrinks or merges a team when one of them changes, and stops creating teams of two or three that cannot survive a holiday or a resignation.
thesis.how_why: Below about four people a team has no redundancy: one absence removes a skill or breaks the rotation. Above about eight, the number of relations inside the team makes it split informally into sub-teams. Larson's rules of thumb are the results of that reasoning for teams that write and operate their own services; the reasoning is what carries over to other situations, the numbers do not. Composition follows from the same concern with waiting: a decision about what to build or how it should work that needs a role the team lacks waits for another team, so the roles such decisions need sit inside the team.

supporting_claims.claim: A team's size is the result of three requirements and not an input: two floors, enough people to understand and change what the team owns without depending on one of them and enough to sustain its on-call rotation, and one ceiling, few enough to coordinate without splitting into sub-teams.

For teams that write and operate their own services the three requirements give Larson's six to eight engineers with one manager; each of his rules of thumb has a stated reason and assumptions, and a different scope, on-call duty or cost of producing a change gives a different number.

A team below one of its floors should grow, shed or share scope and on-call, or merge; headcount added elsewhere does not help, and teams of two or three should not be created because they cannot survive a holiday or a resignation.

Composition follows the same concern with waiting: the roles that decisions about what to build and how it should work need, product, design and engineering and where needed data, sit inside the team, because a decision that needs a role the team lacks waits for another team.

role.contribution: Derives team size and composition, and closes Part II by reading one team as a type, a mode and a size.

additional_patterns.applies_to: floors-and-ceiling, derive-the-size, grow-shed-merge: the requirements come before the steps that apply them, and the derivation before the remedies for a team that fails it

flow.rationale: The reader meets two sizes nobody can explain before any rule. The requirements come next because they answer that puzzle, then the two patterns that use them. Composition follows size because it applies the same reasoning to roles, and it must precede the section on where the sources disagree, which compares Larson's numbers with the Build What Matters ratio that composition introduces. The disagreement among sources and the anti-patterns come only after the reader has the derivation to judge them with. The worked example uses only the requirements and the two patterns; it is placed late, as the page format asks, so that one input of a derivation the reader has just seen run, and the closing of Part II comes last because it needs this chapter's result. Sources first would be numbers with nothing to derive them from.

hook.content: In 2024 every engineer on Corvane's platform team was on call two weeks in every five, and in August, with one colleague on holiday, every second week. The team had five engineers, and nobody at Corvane could say why five.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers lead or work in teams whose size came from a budget line, a division of headcount or a number that was simply never revisited, and have heard six to eight, or two pizzas, quoted as the right answer.
bridge.to_topic: A size that was never derived cannot be defended or corrected; the question is what a team's size should be derived from.

thesis_statement.text: A team should be as large as three things require and no larger: enough people to understand and change what it owns without depending on one of them, enough to sustain its on-call rotation, and few enough to coordinate without splitting into sub-teams. For teams that write and operate their own services that gives Will Larson's six to eight engineers with one manager, and it gives a different number when the scope, the on-call duty or the cost of producing a change is different. Composition follows the same logic: product, design and engineering sit together wherever a decision would otherwise wait for another team.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See two team sizes at Corvane that nobody derived.
Understand the two floors and the ceiling that set a team's size, and where Larson's numbers come from.
Derive a size from a team's scope and on-call duty.
Choose among growing, shedding and merging for a team that is too small.
Decide which roles belong inside the team.
Know where the sources disagree and what a smaller team gives up, and recognize the two usual ways sizing goes wrong.
Size Corvane's platform team, and see which input AI changes.
Close Part II by reading the platform team as a type, a mode and a size.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2024 each of the five engineers on Corvane's platform team was on call two weeks in five, and nobody could say why the team had five engineers or why the product teams had eight.

evidence.what: Corvane, 2024, 180 people: platform team of five engineers on a two-tier on-call rotation, two weeks in five each, every second week in August with one engineer on holiday; five had been the team's size since 2022; the eleven product teams had about eight because about ninety engineers were divided by eleven.
evidence.shows: Both sizes were inputs from history and division, not results of anything the teams had to do.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team should be as large as understanding its scope, sustaining its on-call rotation and coordinating without sub-teams require, which gives six to eight under stated assumptions, and its composition follows the same concern with waiting.

transition_in.carries_over: Two sizes with no reason behind them, and the previous chapters' team types and interaction modes, which decide what a team owns and how much of its time others consume.
transition_in.introduces: How many people and which roles that requires, as one claim, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Two Team Sizes Nobody Derived
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane gave its twelve teams two sizes in 2023, eight by division and five by history; the eight held up and the five did not, and the company could explain neither.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter explains: sizes used as inputs, one of which failed.

flow.rationale: The reader sees where each number came from, then what the smaller one cost in 2024, before the question of what a size should come from is put.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's two numbers, five and eight.
transition_in.introduces: Where each number came from and what five cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2023 Corvane formed eleven product teams of about eight engineers by dividing people evenly and kept its platform team at the five it had had since 2022.

evidence.what: Ledger, stage 3: 95 engineers; eleven product teams of about eight formed in 2023 by dividing people evenly; platform team of five, led by Lena Brandt, formed in 2022 when Corvane had about 45 engineers. New fact: the five was never revisited when the number of engineers it served doubled.
evidence.shows: Neither size was derived from what the team owned or had to sustain.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five engineers on a two-tier rotation meant each was on call two weeks in five, and the same five also did the launch checks every other team waited for.

evidence.what: New ledger facts: the platform team ran a two-tier rotation (primary and secondary) around the clock for the shared infrastructure and the release tooling; each engineer on call two weeks in five; in August 2024 one engineer was on holiday for three weeks and the other four were on call every second week. Ledger: 14 open launch requests at the peak in 2024.
evidence.shows: The cost of five was paid in on-call weeks and in the queue of the previous chapters.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: A team of five that was never re-sized.
transition_in.introduces: What five meant week by week in 2024.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The eight held up and the five did not, and Corvane could explain neither, because both numbers had been inputs to the design and not results of it.

evidence.what: New ledger fact: product teams of about eight ran two-tier rotations for their own services, two weeks in eight each. Ledger: a size from division (ninety by eleven) and a size from history.
evidence.shows: A number that was not derived cannot be defended when it is right or corrected when it is wrong.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: The platform team's five.
transition_in.introduces: The product teams' eight, which worked, and the fact that nobody could say why either.

sections.heading: Two Floors and a Ceiling: What Sets a Team's Size
sections.controlling_idea: A team's size lies between two floors, understanding and on-call, and one ceiling, coordination; for teams that write and operate their own services these meet at Larson's six to eight, and the reasoning carries to other situations where the numbers do not.

advances_thesis.how: States the derivation and shows Larson's rules of thumb as its results under stated assumptions.

flow.rationale: The frame of two floors and a ceiling comes first; each requirement is then taken in turn because the result needs all three; Larson's rules are tabled only after the reasons that produce them, and the limit of the numbers is drawn last.

transition_in.carries_over: Two sizes nobody could explain.
transition_in.introduces: The three requirements a size is derived from.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team's size is a result of three requirements: two floors, set by what the team must understand and by the rotation it must sustain, and one ceiling, set by what it can coordinate; between them, the number depends on how much work the scope demands at the current cost of producing a change.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart LR: "Scope: what the team owns" -> "Understanding floor: every part changeable by at least two people"; "On-call duty" -> "Rotation floor: enough trained people for every tier"; both floors -> "Floor: the higher of the two"; "Coordination inside the team" -> "Ceiling: the size at which sub-teams form"; floor and ceiling -> "Team size: between floor and ceiling"; "Work the scope demands, at the current cost of producing a change" -> team size; edge labeled "floor above ceiling" -> "Too much for one team: shed, share or split". Caption states that size is derived from scope, on-call and coordination, and that a floor above the ceiling means the scope is too large for one team.
evidence.shows: The figure shows size as an output with three inputs, and what it means when the inputs cannot be reconciled.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first floor is understanding: a team needs enough people that every part it owns can be changed without depending on one of them, and below about four it has no redundancy at all.

evidence.what: Chapter 4's ownership test (a team owns a thing only when its members can change and operate it without relying on one particular person) and cognitive load as the measure of what a team must understand.
evidence.shows: The floor is set by scope, not by a general preference for a number.
evidence.source: cognitive-load-and-team-boundaries

evidence.what: Larson: "Teams with fewer than four individuals are a sufficiently leaky abstraction that they function indistinguishably from individuals." He adds that to reason about such a team's delivery you have to know about each on-call shift, vacation and interruption, and that he has regretted every team of one or two he sponsored.
evidence.shows: Below about four, one absence removes a skill, so the unit of planning is the person and not the team.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Two floors and a ceiling.
transition_in.introduces: The first floor and Larson's reason for a minimum of four.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second floor is the on-call rotation: a team that operates its services around the clock needs enough trained people per tier that being on call stays an occasional duty; the author puts the least at six for two tiers (one week in three), and Larson's rule of thumb is eight.

evidence.what: Larson: "My rule of thumb is that it takes eight engineers on a team to support a two-tier on-call rotation". He also notes that only trained engineers can go on call.
evidence.shows: The number is his rule of thumb for one specific duty: two tiers, around the clock.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

evidence.what: The author's arithmetic, not Larson's: with two tiers and n engineers each is on call 2 weeks in n; eight gives one week in four, six one in three, five two in five. The threshold of one week in three, six engineers, is the author's judgement; Larson's eight leaves room for holidays and for engineers still in training.
evidence.shows: Shows why the rotation floor is higher than the understanding floor for teams that operate their own services, and that it moves with the number of tiers and the hours covered.

transition_in.carries_over: The floor set by understanding.
transition_in.introduces: A second floor, set by on-call, with on-call and two-tier rotation defined.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ceiling is coordination: the relations inside a team grow much faster than its headcount, so above about eight a team splits informally into sub-teams and its manager can no longer invest in each person.

evidence.what: Arithmetic: n people have n(n-1)/2 pairs: 5 have 10, 8 have 28, 12 have 66.
evidence.shows: Coordination cost rises faster than size, which is why a ceiling exists.

evidence.what: Larson on managers: managers supporting more than eight or nine engineers typically act as coaches and safety nets, too busy to invest actively in their team or its area of responsibility; managers supporting fewer than four tend to function as tech lead managers who take on a share of design and implementation.
evidence.shows: His six to eight per manager is bounded above by what one manager can invest in and below by the point where the manager becomes a part-time engineer.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Two floors that push the size up.
transition_in.introduces: The ceiling that holds it down.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For teams that write and operate their own services an understanding floor of four, a rotation floor of six at the least and eight to be safe, and a ceiling of about eight give six to eight engineers with one manager, which is Larson's steady-state size, and each of his rules of thumb has a reason and an assumption.

evidence.what: Table of Larson's rules of thumb. Columns: Rule of thumb / His reason / What it assumes. Rows: managers support six to eight engineers (below four the manager becomes a tech lead manager, above eight or nine a coach and safety net; assumes a full-time people manager); three to five engineers when the manager does hands-on technical work (the manager's time is shared; assumes the manager is expected to do hands-on work); about eight engineers for a two-tier on-call rotation (rule of thumb for the rotation; assumes the team operates its own services around the clock in two tiers, with trained engineers); fewer than four is not a team (it functions like individuals; assumes the team is meant to be planned as a unit). The steady-state six to eight is given in the lead-in; growing and budding is in p13.
evidence.shows: Every number is the result of a reason under an assumption, so the reader can tell which numbers apply to their own team.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

evidence.what: Larson: "Teams should be six to eight during steady state."
evidence.shows: The familiar number is his, stated as a steady-state target.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Two floors and a ceiling, each with a reason.
transition_in.introduces: Where they meet for a team that writes and operates its own services, and Larson's rules as the results.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The reasoning carries over to other teams and the numbers do not: change the scope, the on-call duty or the cost of producing a change and the size that comes out is different.

evidence.what: Three variations: a team with no around-the-clock duty has only the understanding floor, so four or five can be right; a team whose manager does hands-on work is three to five by Larson's own rule; a team whose rotation floor is above its coordination ceiling owns too much for one team.
evidence.shows: The same derivation gives different numbers, which is the sense in which six to eight is a result and not a law.

transition_in.carries_over: Six to eight as the result for one kind of team.
transition_in.introduces: What happens to the number when an input changes.

sections.heading: Pattern: Derive the Size from Scope and On-Call
sections.controlling_idea: A size is derived in five steps from the team's scope, its on-call duty, its ceiling and the work the scope demands, and a team reaches that size by growing and splitting, never by being created empty.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the derivation into steps a reader can run, with its user and its outcome measure.

transition_in.carries_over: The three requirements and their reasons.
transition_in.introduces: The steps that apply them to one team.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern's user is the manager of a team and the leader who approves its headcount; its outcome measures are the share of weeks each engineer is on call and the number of parts only one person can change; and it has five steps.

evidence.what: Steps: 1 list what the team owns and operates, part by part; 2 for each part count who can change it safely, and set the understanding floor so that every part has at least two; 3 write down the on-call duty (hours, tiers) and set the rotation floor, using Larson's eight for two tiers around the clock as the starting point; 4 take the higher floor and compare it with the ceiling of about eight engineers with one manager, and between the two add engineers only for the work the scope demands at the current cost of producing a change; 5 if the floor is above the ceiling or above what you can staff, change the scope or the duty, not the arithmetic. Record the assumptions with the result.
evidence.shows: Each step uses one of the three requirements, and the last step sends an impossible result back to scope.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team reaches its derived size by growing from a working team and splitting, never by being assembled empty.

evidence.what: Larson: to create a new team, grow an existing team to eight to ten and then bud into two teams of four or five; never create empty teams. The ten and the four are passing states, briefly above the ceiling and briefly at the understanding floor (the author's gloss).
evidence.shows: New teams start at the understanding floor with habits that already work, and climb back to six to eight.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: A derived size.
transition_in.introduces: How a team gets to that size without being assembled from nothing.

sections.heading: Pattern: Grow, Shed or Merge a Team That Is Too Small
sections.controlling_idea: A team below one of its floors has three remedies, growing, shedding or sharing scope and on-call, and merging, and the choice depends on which floor is broken and on who else could carry the work.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the remedies for a team below its floors and rules out the remedy that does not work.

transition_in.carries_over: A derivation that can show a team is below its floor.
transition_in.introduces: The three remedies and how to choose among them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern's user is the leader responsible for a team below one of its floors, its outcome measure is that the team passes both floors again by a date set with the remedy, and it offers three remedies whose fit depends on which floor is broken.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Remedy / What it changes / What it costs / Fits when. Rows: Grow (raises the team to its floor; months of hiring and training, since only trained engineers go on call; fits when nobody else can understand or operate the scope and the scope will stay). Shed or share scope and on-call (lowers the floor: a service moves to a team that can own it, or the rotation is shared with a team that knows the systems; the receiving team carries more and must learn the systems; fits when part of the scope belongs elsewhere or a neighbouring team already understands it). Merge (two teams below the floor become one above it; one combined scope to understand, one team identity lost; fits when the two scopes are adjacent and neither team can reach its floor alone).
evidence.shows: Each remedy acts on a different term of the derivation: people, scope or duty, or the number of teams.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What does not help is headcount that never reaches the team: people added to other teams, a part-time share of someone who cannot join the rotation, or a person borrowed from a team that then suffers; Larson moves scope instead.

evidence.what: A floor is a property of one team's scope and duty; engineers elsewhere neither understand its parts nor carry its pager. Larson: only trained engineers can go on call.
evidence.shows: Explains why a company can grow overall while one team stays below its floor.

evidence.what: Larson: "I've found it most fruitful to move scope between teams, preserving the teams themselves."
evidence.shows: His alternative to moving people is the shed remedy: the scope moves and the teams stay.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

evidence.what: Larson, on moving people between teams: teams have high fixed costs, so moving one person out can set a healthy team back.
evidence.shows: Borrowing people to patch a small team damages the team they came from, because teams have high fixed costs.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Three remedies that work.
transition_in.introduces: The remedies that look similar and do not.

sections.heading: Composition: The Roles a Decision Would Otherwise Wait For
sections.controlling_idea: A team's composition follows from waiting: the roles its decisions about what to build and how it should work need sit inside the team, in the proportions the work requires, because a decision that needs an absent role waits for another team.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the chapter's reasoning to who is in the team.

flow.rationale: The rule is stated, the roles and the published ratios are tabled as evidence, and Corvane shows what a shared role costs.

transition_in.carries_over: Size derived from what the team must do.
transition_in.introduces: Composition derived the same way, from the decisions the team must make.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A decision about what to build or how it should work that needs a role the team lacks waits for another team, so the roles such decisions need, product, design and engineering, belong inside the team.

evidence.what: Cagan and Jones, Empowered, as recorded in the author's summary: product managers, designers and engineers work as one team, and design treated as an internal service outside the teams starves discovery. Foster and Nerlikar, Build What Matters, as recorded in the author's summary: design works with product as a peer.
evidence.shows: The product sources put the three roles in one team for the reason this chapter gives: decisions otherwise queue.
evidence.source: grounded-product-management: team-topology, right-team

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Which roles a team needs full-time depends on how often its decisions need them, and the published ratio from Build What Matters is a starting point with the same standing as Larson's numbers.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Role / The decisions it brings / Sign that it is missing / Full-time or shared. Rows: Engineering (how to build, change and operate it; nothing ships; the core, sized by the derivation). Product management (which problem is next and what counts as done; engineers guess priorities or wait for an answer; one per team). Design (how it should work for the user; screens wait for a designer or ship undesigned; in the team where the product has a user interface that changes often; shared where it rarely does). Data, where needed (whether a change produced its outcome; nobody can say if a release worked; in the team when its decisions rest on usage data it cannot read itself). Quality assurance appears only in the quoted ratio; where quality engineering sits is left to chapter 16.
evidence.shows: Ties each role to a kind of decision and a visible sign, so that composition can be read off a team's waiting.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: "5 to 7 Developers (your base value) 1 Product Manager 0.5 UX Designer (variable depending on the nature of the product) 0.3 UI Designer (variable depending on the nature of the product) 1 or 2 Quality Assurance Engineers".
evidence.shows: A published ratio that itself says it varies with the nature of the product: a rule of thumb, not a law. The text says that its quality assurance engineers are left to chapter 16 and that the table adds data, which the ratio omits.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: The roles belong in the team.
transition_in.introduces: Which roles, how much of each, and one published ratio.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At Corvane in 2024 every product team had its own product manager and eight of the eleven shared a designer, so in those eight a decision about how a screen should work waited for the designer's days with the team.

evidence.what: Ledger, stage 3: 11 product managers and 7 designers for eleven product teams. New fact: three teams had a designer of their own and four designers each worked for two teams.
evidence.shows: A role shared between teams is a queue for the decisions that need it; the fraction on the plan hides the waiting.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Roles in the proportions the work requires.
transition_in.introduces: What a shared role cost at Corvane.

sections.heading: Where the Sources Disagree: Six to Eight of What, and Why Not Fewer
sections.controlling_idea: The sources give different numbers because they count different things and guard different bounds, and the widely quoted case for the smallest possible team guards only the ceiling; a smaller team gains coordination and gives up redundancy.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the thesis's opponent, that smaller is faster, and states what the familiar numbers count.

flow.rationale: The disagreement is stated, resolved by showing what each source counts, and then the trade the small-team view leaves out is tabled.

transition_in.carries_over: One published ratio and one set of rules of thumb, both used so far as if they agreed.
transition_in.introduces: Where they and the two-pizza rule pull apart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Larson, Build What Matters and the two-pizza rule give three different answers to how large a team should be.

evidence.what: Larson: six to eight engineers per manager. Build What Matters: five to seven developers plus a product manager, parts of two designers and one or two quality assurance engineers, about eight to eleven people. The two-pizza rule, widely attributed to Amazon: a team should be small enough to be fed by two pizzas; cited only as the widely known rule, as a supplement to the author's sources.
evidence.shows: Read as numbers, the sources conflict, and the best known of them says smaller is better.
evidence.source: An Elegant Puzzle; Build What Matters; two-pizza rule (widely known, not from the author's bookshelf)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three count different things and guard different bounds: Larson counts the engineers one manager supports, Build What Matters counts the whole product team around a similar number of engineers, and the two-pizza rule guards only the ceiling.

evidence.what: The book's resolution: the floors and the ceiling of this chapter count engineers, as Larson does, and on that count the ratio's five to seven developers agrees with him; the product manager and designers come on top; a rule that names only a maximum is silent about the floors.
evidence.shows: The sources stop conflicting once each number is attached to what it counts.

transition_in.carries_over: Three numbers that disagree.
transition_in.introduces: What each one counts, and the book's way of using them together.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A smaller team gains easier coordination and gives up redundancy, so smaller is faster only for a team with a narrow scope and no rotation to sustain.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Engineers / What the team gains / What it gives up / Right when. Rows: two or three (almost no coordination; any redundancy: one absence stops a skill or the rotation; a temporary group with an end date, not a standing team). Four or five (little coordination, a hands-on manager; an around-the-clock two-tier rotation, room for a resignation; narrow scope, no such rotation, or a team that has just budded and will grow). Six to eight (redundancy in every part and a sustainable rotation; some coordination cost, a full-time manager; a team that writes and operates its own services).
evidence.shows: Shows what the small-team argument leaves out and the conditions under which it is right.

transition_in.carries_over: A rule that guards only the ceiling.
transition_in.introduces: What each size gains and gives up.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: Sized by Budget, Small on Principle
sections.controlling_idea: Sizing goes wrong in two usual ways: the size is taken from the budget or from division, or teams are kept or created small on principle.

advances_thesis.how: Names the two habits the thesis disputes with the book's failure patterns.

transition_in.carries_over: What each size gains and gives up.
transition_in.introduces: The two habits that ignore that trade.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A size taken from the budget or from dividing headcount gives every team the same number whatever it owns, which leaves the team with the widest scope or the heaviest duty below its floor.

evidence.what: Corvane 2023: eleven teams of about eight by division and a platform team left at five, below its rotation floor; teams cut to fit a number have boundaries that follow the headcount; failure patterns The Org Chart as Architecture and The Overloaded Team.
evidence.shows: The even number was right only where scope and duty happened to match it.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Teams of two or three arise in two ways, created for a new initiative on the belief that small is fast or left behind by a reorganization, and both ways produce a standing team that depends on particular people.

evidence.what: Larson regretted every team of one or two he sponsored. Failure pattern: The Hero Culture.
evidence.shows: The small team's speed is borrowed from the availability of particular people.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: One number for every team.
transition_in.introduces: The opposite habit: the smallest possible team.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Sizing Corvane's Platform Team
sections.controlling_idea: Derived at the end of 2024, the platform team's size comes out at eight: its understanding floor is met at five, its rotation floor is not, growing is the only remedy that fits, and the product teams' eight passes the same test.

advances_thesis.how: Runs the derivation and the choice of remedy on the team the chapter opened with.

flow.rationale: The reader follows the derivation in the order of the pattern's steps: scope, floors and ceiling, remedy, and then the same test on a team whose size was right.

transition_in.carries_over: The derivation, the remedies and the two anti-patterns.
transition_in.introduces: All of them applied to the platform team of the opening.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the end of 2024 the platform team owned three parts, each of which at least two of its five engineers could change, and it was on call for two of them around the clock in two tiers.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Part / Engineers who can change it safely / On-call duty. Rows: release path (automated readiness checks and deployment tooling): 3, two tiers around the clock; shared infrastructure (hosting, databases, monitoring): 3, two tiers around the clock; shared data model for customers and jobs: 2, working hours. New ledger facts; the launch checks themselves had left the team with the 2024 release path.
evidence.shows: Gives the inputs of the derivation: scope part by part, who understands it, and the duty.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The derivation gives eight: the understanding floor is met at five, the rotation floor is not (five is below the least of six; six leaves nothing for a holiday or an engineer in training, so the floor taken for this team is Larson's eight), the ceiling is about eight, and the work the scope demands calls for no more.

evidence.what: Understanding floor: every part has at least two people, so five passes. Rotation floor: two tiers around the clock; six at the least, and Larson's eight taken for this team because of holidays and training (August 2024). Ceiling: about eight engineers with one manager. Floor and ceiling meet at eight.
evidence.shows: Five was wrong for one identifiable reason, the rotation, and not in general.

transition_in.carries_over: The team's scope and duty.
transition_in.introduces: The size they require.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Of the three remedies only growing fitted, so Corvane hired three platform engineers in the first half of 2025, and each joined the rotation only after training.

evidence.what: New ledger facts: Lena Brandt proposed and Dario Vance approved growing the platform team from five to eight in the plan for 2025; shedding the rotation was rejected because no product team understood the shared infrastructure; merging was rejected because no team had an adjacent scope; a single tier was rejected because a missed alert would stop every team's releases; three engineers joined in the first half of 2025 and joined the rotation after a quarter each; by the end of 2025 each engineer was on call two weeks in eight. Scope had already been shed once, in 2024, when the launch checks moved to the product teams.
evidence.shows: The choice among remedies follows from which floor was broken and who else could carry the work; the outcome measure moved from two weeks in five to two in eight.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: A floor of eight and a team of five.
transition_in.introduces: The remedy chosen and why the other two did not fit.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same test explains why the product teams' eight had worked: Scheduling, with eight engineers and a two-tier rotation for its own services, met both floors and sat at the ceiling.

evidence.what: Ledger: Scheduling, eight engineers; after the 2025 re-cut four engineers could change the job-status rules (one before). New facts: two-tier rotation for its own services, two weeks in eight; after the re-cut no part that only one engineer could change.
evidence.shows: The eight from division was right by coincidence of scope and duty, and the derivation is what says so.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: The platform team derived.
transition_in.introduces: A product team put through the same derivation.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: AI changes one input of the derivation, the cost of producing a change, and leaves the two floors and the ceiling to be applied again; which way the number moves is not yet known.

advances_thesis.how: Names the input the journal thesis says AI changes and labels every claim about it.

transition_in.carries_over: A derivation with stated inputs, run for Corvane in 2024.
transition_in.introduces: The one input coding agents change.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Coding agents lower the cost of producing a change, which is the input that decided how many engineers a given scope needed, and they leave the understanding floor and the rotation floor where they were.

evidence.what: Labeled Emerging, the author's observation as of November 2026: agents add capacity for writing changes. The floors do not count hands that write: one counts people who understand each part, the other trained people on a rotation.
evidence.shows: Locates the change in one input and shows why the familiar number does not simply fall.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What follows is speculative: a team may own a wider scope at the same size, or teams may settle nearer the floors, and the limit is then what the team can understand and verify.

evidence.what: Labeled Speculative; would be confirmed where organizations with agents in every team report stable teams of four or five that sustain their rotations (for example through shared rotations), or teams of six to eight owning measurably more without more parts known to one person. Full argument in team-shape-and-roles-with-ai.
evidence.shows: States what is not known and what evidence would settle it.

transition_in.carries_over: One input changed and two floors unchanged.
transition_in.introduces: What may happen to team size, and what would confirm it.

sections.heading: Closing Part II: One Team Read as a Type, a Mode and a Size
sections.controlling_idea: Type, mode and size are one decision made three times, and Corvane's platform team was the right type with the wrong mode and too few people for its scope, none of which the org chart showed.

advances_thesis.how: Carries the closing the journal spec assigns to this chapter for Part II: synthesis, so-what and callback to the part's opening.

transition_in.carries_over: This chapter's derivation, applied to Corvane and to AI.
transition_in.introduces: The same team read with all three chapters of Part II.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read with the three chapters of Part II, Corvane's platform team of 2024 was the right type, in the wrong mode, with too few people for its scope.

evidence.what: Table. Columns: Reading / What the team should have been / What it was in 2024 / Shown on the org chart? Rows: Type (chapter 6): a platform team, which exists to take mechanics off the teams that deliver to users / a platform team / only the name. Mode (chapter 7): X-as-a-Service, the product teams releasing without asking / a request for a launch, a collaboration nobody chose that had become a queue / no. Size (this chapter): eight for its rotation, or a smaller duty / five / the number, not the reason.
evidence.shows: One team, three readings, each wrong or right independently, and none of them visible in a box with five names.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json entries team-types, interaction-modes-and-team-apis, part-2 closing; _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three readings are one decision made three times: what a team is for decides how others should reach it, and both decide how many people it needs.

evidence.what: Part II's closing synthesis. A platform team that serves through a service needs people to build and operate the service; one that serves through requests needs people in proportion to the requests; Corvane changed the mode in 2024 and only then could the size be derived. Callback to the part's opening: the team of five created to help eleven teams release faster.
evidence.shows: Type, mode and size cannot be settled one at a time, which is why the part's takeaway asks for all three per team.

transition_in.carries_over: Three readings of one team.
transition_in.introduces: Why they are one decision, and the part's opening team seen again.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: A team size is an answer with its working shown: the floors come from what the team owns and must sustain, the ceiling from what it can coordinate, and the roles from the decisions it must make. The same reasoning that sizes a team says what to do when the size is wrong, and Part II as a whole says that type, mode and size are one decision made three times.
conclusion.so_what: The reader can state the assumptions behind a team's size, tell whether a team that is too small should grow, shed scope or merge, stop creating teams of two or three, and re-derive the number when scope, on-call duty or the cost of producing a change moves.

callback.to: The platform team of five, on call two weeks in five, whose size nobody could explain; and Part II's opening, the team created to help eleven teams release faster.
callback.how: The reader can now say why five was wrong (the rotation floor), why eight was right for the product teams, and can read the same team as a type, a mode and a size.

takeaway.content: List your teams with a type, the mode of each of their main interactions, and the reason for each team's size; where the reason is missing, derive it. The checklist gives the steps.
